subject: English
description: Affirmative ↔ negative, simple ↔ complex, degrees of comparison, exclamatory ↔ assertive

questions.stem: Choose the correct affirmative form of: 'No man is happy without health.'

options.option_text: Every man without health is happy.
Every man with health is happy.
All men are unhappy with health.
Some men are happy without health.

questions.explanation: Negative ('No man... without...') has TWO negatives — they cancel out. So the statement means 'Every man WITH health is happy'. Rule for double-negation: 'No X is Y without Z' ≡ 'Every X with Z is Y'. Useful related transformations — 'None but X' ≡ 'Only X', 'Not less than' ≡ 'At least'.

questions.stem: Transform into a complex sentence: 'I know his address.'

options.option_text: I know his address and his phone number.
I know where he lives.
Knowing his address, I called him.
His address is known to me.

questions.explanation: Complex sentence = 1 main clause + 1+ subordinate clauses joined by subordinating conjunctions (where, when, that, because, although, if, since…). 'I know his address' (simple) → 'I know where he lives' (complex — subordinate noun clause 'where he lives'). Compound = two independent clauses joined by FANBOYS (and, but, or…).

questions.stem: Transform 'Mumbai is the largest city in India' into a comparative degree sentence.

options.option_text: Mumbai is as large as any other city in India.
Mumbai is larger than any other city in India.
No city in India is large.
Mumbai is large like other cities in India.

questions.explanation: Three degrees of comparison: positive ('No other city in India is AS LARGE AS Mumbai'); comparative ('Mumbai is LARGER THAN ANY OTHER city in India'); superlative ('Mumbai is THE LARGEST city in India'). Note 'any OTHER' is essential when comparing within a group — without 'other', a thing would be compared to itself.

questions.stem: Transform 'How beautifully she sings!' into an assertive (declarative) sentence.

options.option_text: She does not sing well.
She sings very beautifully.
She is beautiful when she sings.
She is a beautiful singer.

questions.explanation: Exclamatory → Assertive: replace 'How / What a' with 'very' (or 'so / extremely') + drop the exclamation mark + adjust word order to subject-verb-rest. 'How beautifully she sings!' → 'She sings very beautifully.' Other examples: 'What a fool he is!' → 'He is a great fool.' 'How tall the building is!' → 'The building is very tall.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct interrogative form of: 'Everybody likes ice-cream.'

options.option_text: Does everybody like ice-cream?
Who does not like ice-cream?
Why does everybody like ice-cream?
How is ice-cream liked?

questions.explanation: An assertive sentence with universal quantifier ('everybody', 'no one') is best transformed into a rhetorical question of OPPOSITE polarity. 'Everybody likes' (positive universal) → 'Who does NOT like?' (negative interrogative — same meaning). Conversely 'No one likes' → 'Who likes?'. Direct 'Does everybody like?' shifts the meaning to a yes/no inquiry, not the universal claim.

questions.stem: Transform 'As soon as he saw the police, he ran away.' to start with 'No sooner...'

options.option_text: No sooner did he see the police than he ran away.
No sooner he saw the police than he ran away.
No sooner he had seen the police, then he ran away.
No sooner he saw the police but he ran away.

questions.explanation: Standard 'No sooner ... than ...' construction requires AUXILIARY INVERSION + 'than' (NOT 'then'). 'No sooner DID he see the police THAN he ran away.' Common errors: forgetting the inversion ('No sooner he saw' is wrong); using 'when' or 'but' instead of 'than'; using 'then' (a temporal adverb) instead of 'than' (a comparison conjunction).

questions.stem: Pick the correct passive form: 'They will finish the project tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The project will finish tomorrow.
The project will be finished by them tomorrow.
The project is finished tomorrow.
The project has been finished tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Future Indefinite passive: subject + will be + V3 (past participle) + by + agent. 'They will finish' → 'will be finished'. Object 'project' becomes new subject; the doer 'they' becomes 'by them' (often dropped if obvious). Future Continuous passive doesn't exist in standard usage. Future Perfect: 'will have finished' → 'will have been finished'.

questions.stem: Which option correctly rewrites 'She was too nervous to speak clearly during the interview' using 'so...that'?

options.option_text: She was so nervous that she could speak clearly during the interview.
She was so nervous that she could not speak clearly during the interview.
She was so nervous so she could not speak clearly during the interview.
She was so nervous that she may not speak clearly during the interview.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'too + adjective + to + verb' converts to 'so + adjective + that + subject + cannot + verb.' The infinitive 'to speak' becomes 'could not speak.' Option A reverses the meaning entirely. Option C uses 'so...so' which is an ungrammatical double-connector. Option D uses 'may not,' implying mere possibility rather than inability, which changes the original meaning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct passive form of 'The government has launched several welfare schemes for the rural poor'?

options.option_text: Several welfare schemes were launched by the government for the rural poor.
Several welfare schemes have been launched by the government for the rural poor.
Several welfare schemes are launched by the government for the rural poor.
Several welfare schemes had been launched by the government for the rural poor.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the active voice uses present perfect tense ('has launched'), whose passive equivalent is 'have/has been + past participle' → 'have been launched.' Option A uses simple past ('were launched'), which changes the tense. Option C uses simple present ('are launched'), losing the perfect aspect. Option D uses past perfect ('had been launched'), which implies an action completed before another past event — a different tense altogether.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly transforms 'The suspect refused to confess unless his lawyer was present' into an 'if...not' conditional?

options.option_text: The suspect refused to confess if his lawyer was not present.
The suspect refused to confess if his lawyer would not be present.
The suspect refused not to confess if his lawyer was present.
The suspect refused to confess if his lawyer had not been present.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'unless P' = 'if not P' with tense preserved — 'unless his lawyer was present' → 'if his lawyer was not present.' Option B introduces 'would,' creating a modal conditional that alters the original meaning. Option C shifts the negation to 'refused,' producing a double-negative error ('refused not to confess') that reverses the meaning. Option D shifts to past perfect ('had not been present'), which implies a time-sequence relationship not present in the original.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts 'The Ganga flows faster than any other river in India' to superlative degree?

options.option_text: The Ganga flows most fast among all rivers in India.
The Ganga flows the fastest of all rivers in India.
The Ganga is fastest flowing than all rivers in India.
No river in India flows as fast as the Ganga flows.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'faster than any other' in comparative becomes 'the fastest of all' in superlative. Option A uses 'most fast,' which is incorrect — the irregular superlative of 'fast' is 'fastest,' not 'most fast.' Option C wrongly combines superlative form 'fastest' with the comparative connector 'than' — superlatives do not take 'than.' Option D correctly expresses the idea but in positive degree ('as fast as'), not superlative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly converts 'Although the evidence was compelling, the jury acquitted the accused' into a compound sentence?

options.option_text: The evidence was compelling, but the jury acquitted the accused still.
The evidence was compelling, yet the jury acquitted the accused.
The evidence was compelling, so the jury acquitted the accused.
The evidence being compelling, the jury acquitted the accused.

questions.explanation: B is correct: the concessive subordinating conjunction 'although' converts to the coordinating conjunction 'yet' to form a compound sentence expressing contrast. Option A uses 'but...still' — while 'but' is valid, placing 'still' at the end is ungrammatical (it must precede the verb). Option C uses 'so,' which implies a causal consequence, completely inverting the meaning. Option D uses a participial phrase ('being compelling'), which produces a simple sentence, not a compound one.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly transforms 'She had scarcely reached the station when the train departed' using an inverted (negative-adverb fronted) structure?

options.option_text: Scarcely had she reached the station when the train departed.
Scarcely she had reached the station when the train departed.
Scarcely had she reached the station than the train departed.
Scarcely did she reach the station when the train departed.

questions.explanation: A is correct: fronting 'scarcely' triggers subject-auxiliary inversion → 'Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when.' Option B places the auxiliary after the subject ('she had'), failing to invert — a very common error. Option C uses 'than' after 'scarcely,' which is incorrect; 'than' belongs to the 'no sooner...than' pattern — 'scarcely/hardly' always pairs with 'when.' Option D uses 'did...reach' (simple past), but the original has past perfect ('had reached'); inversion must preserve the original tense.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly transforms the Type 3 conditional 'If he had invested wisely in his youth, he would not have struggled financially in old age' into a Type 2 conditional?

options.option_text: If he invests wisely in his youth, he will not struggle financially in old age.
If he invested wisely in his youth, he would not struggle financially in old age.
If he had been investing wisely in his youth, he would not struggle financially.
If he would have invested wisely, he would not have struggled financially in old age.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Type 3 (if + past perfect ... would have + V3) expresses a counterfactual past; Type 2 (if + simple past ... would + V1) expresses a hypothetical present/future. The conversion requires 'had invested' → 'invested' and 'would not have struggled' → 'would not struggle.' Option A converts to Type 1 (real future), not Type 2. Option C uses past continuous ('had been investing') in the if-clause — neither Type 2 nor a valid inversion. Option D places 'would have' inside the if-clause, which is a widespread Indian-English error; 'would' never appears in the if-clause of standard conditionals.
